lesson.title: Smooth Waves: Why Sine and Cosine Never Skip a Beat
lesson.summary: Sine and cosine are continuous at every real number, and this fact, combined with the quotient law, pins down exactly where tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant remain continuous.
lesson.body:
The graphs of sine and cosine are smooth, unbroken waves, and that visual smoothness is not just an artifact of how graphing software draws them. It is a theorem: sine and cosine are continuous at every real number. Establishing this fact, and then understanding what happens to the other four trigonometric functions built from them, completes the picture of continuity for the standard function families used throughout calculus.

The key building block is the limit of sine at 0. Using the bound that the absolute value of sin x never exceeds the absolute value of x for any real x, you can squeeze sin x toward 0 as x approaches 0, which combined with cos x approaching 1 gives continuity of sine and cosine at the single point x = 0. To extend this to every point a, use the angle addition identity sin(a + h) = sin(a)cos(h) + cos(a)sin(h). As h approaches 0, cos(h) approaches 1 and sin(h) approaches 0, so sin(a + h) approaches sin(a)(1) + cos(a)(0) = sin(a). A parallel argument using cos(a + h) = cos(a)cos(h) - sin(a)sin(h) shows cosine is continuous at every a as well.

With sine and cosine continuous everywhere, the remaining four trigonometric functions inherit their continuity from the quotient law, exactly as rational functions inherited continuity from polynomials. Since tan x = sin x / cos x and sec x = 1/cos x, both are continuous wherever cos x is not zero, which excludes x = pi/2 + k*pi for any integer k. Since cot x = cos x / sin x and csc x = 1/sin x, both are continuous wherever sin x is not zero, which excludes x = k*pi for any integer k.

For a worked example of continuity holding, check f(x) = sin(x)cos(x) at x = pi/4. Direct substitution gives f(pi/4) = sin(pi/4)cos(pi/4) = (square root of 2 over 2) times (square root of 2 over 2) = 2/4 = 1/2. Since sin and cos are each continuous at pi/4, the product law for continuity guarantees the limit of f(x) as x approaches pi/4 also equals 1/2, matching f(pi/4) exactly, so f is continuous there, as it is at every real number.

For a worked example of continuity breaking, examine tan x near x = pi/2, where cos(pi/2) = 0. As x approaches pi/2 from the left, sin x approaches 1 while cos x approaches 0 through positive values, so the ratio sin x / cos x grows without bound toward positive infinity. As x approaches pi/2 from the right, cos x approaches 0 through negative values, so the ratio plunges toward negative infinity. This infinite discontinuity at x = pi/2 mirrors the vertical asymptote seen for rational functions like (x + 1)/(x - 1), and it produces the vertical asymptote visible on every graph of the tangent function.

So the takeaway is a clean split: sine and cosine have no exceptions at all, continuous on the entire real line, while tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant are continuous everywhere except at the specific angles where their defining denominator vanishes. The same factor-based reasoning used for rational functions applies here directly, just with sin x and cos x playing the role of the numerator and denominator polynomials.
